job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk at an insurance company in Ottawa by eight-thirty. I work on the claims system, which is old software that handles people's car and home claims, and I mostly fix bugs and make small changes. My team lead Mr Dubois hands out the tickets, and Karen, a senior developer, sits next to me and explains the old code. I finished software engineering last summer with a plain pass and no internship. In the evening I see my fiancée Rita, a primary school teacher, and on Sundays we go to church and then to my parents' grocery shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, steady as she goes. People who build real things and look after real customers still matter. At work I'd say it's fine, and I'd tell my dad at the shop that nothing's changing, which would make him smile. I wouldn't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly I'd be relieved. The claims system will always need people who understand it, because nobody wants to touch it. Still, I have a 22,000 dollar loan, and Rita and I want a wedding in two years, which costs about 25,000. If nothing changes with AI, my job is fine, but the loan and the wedding are tight enough on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing claims bugs and learning the old code from Karen. I'd save 500 dollars a month toward the wedding, keep the loan payments steady, and take the Java certification the company pays for. I'd use the chatbot a bit for explaining code, as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Steady. A little stretched, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does tight look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is 700 for my share of the basement flat, the loan payment is 350, and I save 500 for the wedding. That leaves less than I'd like for fun, and Rita's pay as a teacher is modest. We don't complain, but we count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rita say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we have each other and God, and the rest will come. She's more relaxed than me. But she also tells me to ask for a raise, since I'm too polite to ask.

say: I'd say good, steady as she goes: people who look after **real customers** still matter.
I'd tell my dad at the shop that nothing's changing.
think: The claims system always needs people who understand it, since **nobody** wants to touch it.
The **22,000 dollar** loan and a 25,000 dollar wedding are tight on their own.
do: Keep fixing bugs and learning the old code from **Karen**.
Save **500 dollars** a month toward the wedding.
feel: Steady but a little **stretched**, though okay.

fieldNote: Pressure is the **wedding budget** and loan, not AI.

steps.text: Keep fixing claims bugs and learning old code from Karen
Save 500 dollars a month for the wedding

Keep the wedding date but cap the budget at 25,000 dollars

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll adapt, as people have before. Some jobs change and that's life, as long as firms take responsibility for their people. At work I'd say let's learn it and do the job better. At church I'd just say I'm keeping my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing bugs and making small changes in a big old system is the kind of thing AI does well. I think the company will hire fewer developers and expect more from the ones who stay. I'm a plain-pass junior, so I'd have to prove I'm worth keeping. It's one thing to say that and another to feel it at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more and make sure Mr Dubois sees it. I'd ask Karen to teach me the parts of the system she carries in her head, because that's knowledge a tool can't read. I'd save 600 dollars a month, and keep the wedding date but make the guest list smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like a shift in the weather: nothing falls on you yet, but you look at the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the smaller guest list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather have a modest wedding and a safe job than a big wedding and a debt. My mum would be upset, since she wants a hundred and fifty people. A wedding is one day and a marriage is the rest of our lives, so I'd rather have a modest wedding and a safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He runs a grocery, so he thinks everything is about margins. He says a person who works hard and saves will be fine in any economy. I like that, but a shop can't pay two people a graduate's salary, so I have no fallback there. I'd help on weekends, though.

say: I'd say we'll **adapt**, as long as firms take responsibility for their people.
At church I'd say I'm keeping my head down.
think: Bug fixes in a big old system are what AI does well, so the firm may hire **fewer developers**.
As a plain-pass junior I'd have to prove I'm worth keeping.
do: Use the tools more and make sure **Mr Dubois** sees it.
Ask Karen to teach me what only **she** knows about the system.
Save 600 dollars a month and cut the wedding guest list.
feel: Anxious, like a **weather** shift: nothing falls yet but you watch the sky.
S1.quote: A wedding is one day and a marriage is the rest of our lives, so I'd rather have a modest wedding and a safe job.
fieldNote: Moves to the tools **visibly** and absorbs senior knowledge.
Willing to shrink the wedding before risking debt.
Family shop is no fallback, only weekend help.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant on every ticket and show Mr Dubois the results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's irresponsible to move this fast, and governments should make firms slow down or pay for the damage. At work I'd say let's be useful and see. At church I'd ask people to pray and to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the claims team goes within two years, mostly. Software that can read old code and fix it is just the kind of thing the company would buy. I'd be one of the first to go, as the newest, and Rita's pay can't carry us. It would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I can: eating out, the car insurance upgrade, the gym. I'd save 800 dollars a month and put the wedding off by a year if I had to. I'd ask my dad for weekend hours at the shop, and look for jobs that involve people, like IT support at a hospital. And I'd lean on the church group, since they've helped people before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums. I keep thinking about letting Rita down, which I know is silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would it feel like letting her down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I told my fiancée's father I'd provide. If I lost my job, it would feel like breaking a promise to a man I respect, even if it's not my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the wedding had to be delayed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still be engaged, which is what counts. Rita would be upset but she'd understand. We'd tell the families together, and I'd ask my priest to talk to us. I think a delayed wedding is easier to survive than a rushed marriage with no income.

say: I'd say it's irresponsible to move this fast, and firms should **slow down** or pay for the damage.
At church I'd ask people to pray and look after each other.
think: The claims team goes within **two years**, and as the newest I'd be one of the first.
Rita's teaching pay can't carry us both.
do: Cut eating out, the gym and the car insurance upgrade, and save **800 dollars** a month.
Ask my dad for **weekend hours** at the grocery.
Delay the wedding a year and lean on my church group.
feel: Alarmed, lying awake doing **sums** and fearing I'd let Rita down.
S2.quote: I told my fiancée's father I'd provide. If I lost my job, it would feel like breaking a promise to a man I respect, even if it's not my fault.
fieldNote: His alarm is about **honour**: a promise to provide.
Would delay the wedding rather than rush into a marriage with no income.
Turns to church and family before the state.

steps.text: Stop eating out and skip the car insurance upgrade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do it properly, and people should use it to train and save. At work I'd say let's learn the new tools. At church I'd say look after your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'd be 27, probably married with a small child, and the claims jobs might be mostly gone. But I'd have five years to move into something else, like systems that need people to explain them to customers. I'm hopeful, and a bit tense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the Java certification and then a cloud one, save 600 dollars a month, and keep the wedding date in two years. I'd learn the AI tools properly, since I'll need them, and look for a role at my company that deals with clients. I'd put some money into a small index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd keep an eye on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which clock do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The baby clock. My fiancée and I want children within five years. If AGI arrives in 2031, a child would be one or two, the hardest time to lose income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should keep the shop, because a shop with loyal customers is a rare thing. I'd tell him I may need to lean on him a bit, and he'd say he's been waiting for that day, because he wants to help.

say: I'd say we have **time** to do it properly, and people should use it to train and save.
At church I'd say look after your neighbours.
think: By 2031 I'd be **27**, probably married with a small child, and claims jobs might be mostly gone.
I'd have five years to move into client-facing systems work.
do: Do the Java and then a **cloud** certification, saving 600 dollars a month.
Keep the **wedding** date in two years.
Seek a client-facing role at my company and start a small index fund.
feel: Uneasy, not scared, with one eye on the **clock**.
S3.quote: My fiancée and I want children within five years. If AGI arrives in 2031, a child would be one or two, the hardest time to lose income.
fieldNote: Family timing is the **clock** that matters most.

steps.text: Pass the Java and cloud certifications within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a good long time. I'd say people should keep working and saving and not panic. At work I'd say nothing. At church I'd say it's in God's hands, and that's a comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 32 with kids and a decade of experience. Maybe I'd be a team lead who understands both the old systems and the new tools. The one thing I'd watch is the cost of living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, save, get married and buy a small house within five years. I'd use AI tools more as they prove themselves. And I'd put money into a family savings plan for the kids' school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, hopeful. It looks like the life I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get comfortable. A decade makes people lazy, so I'd keep a rule of one new thing a year, a course or a tool, and I'd never be more than a year behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope the world looks like then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One where families still have time together, and where firms still look after their workers. If machines do the work and the owners keep all the money, that's not a good world. I'd want people to have dignity and a job to do, even if the job is different.

say: I'd say people should keep **working and saving** and not panic.
At church I'd say it's in God's hands, and that's a comfort.
think: By 2036 I'd be **32** with kids and ten years of experience, maybe a team lead.
The one thing to watch is the **cost of living**.

Use AI tools more as they prove themselves.

feel: Calm and hopeful, since it looks like the **life** I want.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Rita and I would be in the middle of planning a wedding and a life, and I'd be a plain-pass junior with a loan. What would help is the company being honest, a church and community that look after people, and a government that rewards firms that keep their workers. Some time would help most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of work. I'll work two jobs if I have to. What scares me is not being allowed to work, because work is how I look after my family.

headlineQuote: What scares me is not being allowed to work, because work is how I look after my family.
portrait: **David**, 22, fixes bugs in an Ottawa insurer's claims system, with a **22,000 dollar** loan and a wedding to plan.
Traditional and market-minded, he trusts **work**, family and church, and uses AI tools now and then.
Claims-system coding is the kind of work AI takes early, so his mood climbs to **alarmed** at two years.
What drives him is a promise to **provide** for his fiancée, which turns a job threat into a question of honour.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, with a wedding to plan and a plain-pass junior's job at risk.
whatWouldHelp: A company that is **honest** early, and a community that looks after people.
Time to prepare, and rules that reward firms that keep **workers**.
